items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: T-Bone drove me, Buster and someone else to the gig

ctx.x: Kirby got a gig in some town near L.A. to do a concert which also featured T-Bone Walker and Red Nichols with his Five Pennies. I used to buy records by Red when I was still an amateur and I picked up a few things from him although I didn't strictly go for his style.

T-Bone drove me, Buster and someone else to the gig and we smoked some gage going. I got more of a kick out of hearing Red Nichols for the first time in person than I did from the old records I had of him. Red had been living in California for years and was almost a forgotten legend.

T-Bone went on before us and when we closed the show, he had left and gone back to Lost Angeles. We had to get back the best way we could and I put T-Bone on my S--T list, even if he was a good blues musician.

items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I had heard of T-Bone, but never seen him in action... T-Bone drove me, Buster and someone else to the gig

ctx.x: After a week in Los Angeles we went to work at the Plantation Club which was a few miles outside of the city limits. The jumpingest part of Los Angeles for Negros was around Central Avenue. But it was only possible to get a taxi from the railroad station to your destination when you arrived in town, because of the war conditions. It took such a long time to get to Central avenue from where we were living, by any other means of transportation except private car, that most of us had no desire to go to that part of…

Kirby hired a big car to take us to the plantation which I remember as taking about two and a half hours to get there. And that was how I saw Central Avenue, because we passed there going and coming from the Plantation. On the bill with Kirby's orchestra was T-Bone Walker and Betty Roché, the ex-Ellington singer. I had heard of T-Bone, but never seen him in action and I must say, that he was the best blues singer to accompany himself on electric guitar that I've ever heard. And Betty was still a great vocalist.…

There were four people in Los Angeles that I had known back East: Herb Fleming, who was the trombonist in my unsuccessful adventure as orchestra leader, Inez Cavanaugh, the wife of Timmie Rosenkrantz who had been my manager, and Zutty Singleton, who had come to New York with Louis Armstrong and stayed there for years before going West. Also Benny Carter, my old boss and friend from way back. It was certainly nice to see someone that I knew from New York which was back home to me.
